name: Deltoid / shoulder implants

lead: The idea is to place a solid implant over the deltoid region to make the shoulders look broader and rounder, building the wide-shoulder, V-shaped upper-body look discussed in hardmaxxing circles.

The implant adds volume that changes the shoulder outline directly, rather than building muscle. No published study of implants used purely for shoulder appearance was found; shoulder implant research covers joint replacement for arthritis, fractures and rotator cuff disease.

paras: It is a surgical procedure done by a surgeon, discussed as an alternative to years of shoulder training. Results would be visible once healing finishes.

As with any surgical implant, complications such as infection are documented in the joint-replacement literature. The risks of a cosmetic shoulder implant have not been studied in the sources reviewed, and the procedure involves surgery and anesthesia.

angle.text: Discussed in hardmaxxing circles as a surgical way to add width and roundness to the shoulders for a V-shaped upper body. The implant adds volume over the deltoid, so the contour change is visible directly. Published implant research concerns joint replacement rather than cosmetic use.

lead: Deltoid or shoulder implants are a cosmetic surgical idea in which a solid implant is placed over or within the shoulder region to widen and round the shoulder outline. The deltoid is the muscle that forms the rounded contour of the shoulder and is the prime mover of arm abduction.[1] Broad, rounded shoulders are among the proportions discussed in appearance communities as part of a V-shaped upper body, where shoulder width is set against the waist; people who want that look and have not reached it through training are the audience for the idea.

The route to that look that appears most often alongside the idea is a visible deltoid, which can be built through resistance training such as lateral raises and overhead pressing, and which has been studied in the exercise-science literature for how much each shoulder muscle contributes to arm elevation [2]. An implant would work differently: it would add volume to the outline rather than enlarge the muscle itself.

A plastic surgeon who writes about the procedure, Barry Eppley, states that there are no true preformed deltoid implants, so they are custom made, and that a patient's goal is often width to improve the waist-to-shoulder balance rather than more muscle bulk.[3] Published peer-reviewed research on cosmetic deltoid implants has not been located; the surgical literature on shoulder implants concerns joint replacement (arthroplasty) for arthritis, fractures and rotator cuff disease, a different purpose and procedure.[4][5][6]
infobox: Deltoid: anterior, intermediate and posterior heads [1]

paras: The deltoid has anterior (clavicular), intermediate (acromial) and posterior (scapular) heads, arising from the clavicle, acromion and scapular spine and converging on the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus; together these fibers give the shoulder its rounded outline [1]. The name comes from the Greek letter delta, which the muscle resembles, and "delt" is the common slang [1]. In a study of 30 shoulders the muscle averaged about 192 g, with a range from 84 g to 366 g [1]. The axillary nerve, with roots from C5 and C6, supplies it [1].

Visible shoulder width in a person is also influenced by the skeleton, notably the clavicles, which is why appearance discussions often separate bone width from muscle and soft-tissue volume. The deltoid works with the rotator cuff: estimates of abduction torque attribute a large share to the middle deltoid alongside the supraspinatus, infraspinatus and subscapularis [2].

sections.h: Implants in the shoulder: joint replacement
paras: Most published work on shoulder implants concerns prostheses that replace the glenohumeral joint. Shoulder replacement dates to the 1890s, when Jules-Emile Pean pioneered a procedure; Charles Neer performed the first humeral hemiarthroplasty in 1955, and reverse total shoulder arthroplasty developed in the 1980s, with Paul Grammont's 1985 technique underlying most reverse procedures today [7].

Examples in the research literature include a laboratory study of how reverse shoulder implant design affects abduction range of motion [4], a Norwegian register study of 1,825 shoulder arthroplasties and their revision risk [5], telemeterized implants that measured joint loads in patients during daily activities [8][9], and overviews of periprosthetic infection [6]. These prostheses sit inside the joint and are chosen for pain relief and function; they are not designed to change outward shoulder appearance.

Surgical reports describe the deltoid as an important structure for these procedures: the deltopectoral approach preserves the deltoid, while a transdeltoid approach gives direct access to the socket but puts the deltoid and axillary nerve at risk [7]. Overview sources report complication rates near 5 percent depending on procedure type, with implant loosening, cuff insufficiency, instability and infection among the causes of failure [7]. These figures concern medical arthroplasty patients and are not data on cosmetic implants.

Descriptions of cosmetic deltoid augmentation come from practising plastic surgeons rather than from trials. Eppley's Q&A pages say that implants are custom-made, that the size is limited by the length of the incision used to insert them and by how far the overlying fascia can stretch, and that muscle growth after placement adds to the overall effect.[3] He also says there is a limit to how much shoulder width looks pleasing, and that the more important aim is an implant that blends with surrounding tissue at any size.[3]

The same pages address the difference between implant width and muscle size: Eppley writes that implants create an 'indistinct mass effect', so the two are not cleanly separable.[3] The main concern he raises is visibility, because the deltoid has a thin layer of tissue over it and low body fat may reveal the implant's outline.[3] These accounts are one surgeon's practice statements; no complication rates or long-term outcome series for cosmetic deltoid implants have been published in the research located.

Intramuscular injections are usually given in the lower half of the deltoid because the axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus, and the nerve can be injured in axillary surgery or shoulder dislocation; the same nerve is what any procedure around the deltoid must avoid.[1] Deltoid size can also fall with disuse, denervation and ageing, which is another reason people seek volume at the shoulder.[1]

Resistance-training literature describes the deltoid's role in common shoulder exercises, with electromyography work showing different contributions from the deltoid heads and rotator cuff muscles across exercises [2]. Lateral raises rely mainly on the intermediate fibers, and rowing movements load the posterior fibers [1]. Lifting forums such as T Nation host routine discussions about shoulder training and overhead pressing, including comparisons of kettlebell and barbell pressing muscle activity [10].

No studies found. Studies of shoulder arthroplasty exist, including a laboratory study of reverse implant design, a Norwegian register series of 1,825 arthroplasties and registered trials of reverse versus total replacement, but they concern joint replacement for medical indications, not cosmetic enlargement of the deltoid or shoulder contour.[4][5][6]
